source: Bhushan, Zhang, Wang (2026) Can LLM Agents Discover? Evaluating Creativity on ML Engineering Tasks
finding: Uses Boden's P-creativity and H-creativity as a 0-4 rubric (routine to transformational) to score agent episodes on 10 MLE-Bench tasks. A GPT-5 judge tracks human labels well.
numbers: 300 episodes labelled by 3 trained annotators, Krippendorff alpha 0.724 (ordinal). Judge Spearman with humans: GPT-5 0.732, GLM-5 0.703, DeepSeek V3.2 0.700, Qwen3-235B 0.685, GPT-OSS-120B 0.544. Embedding nearest-neighbour 0.637, centroid 0.589, mean 0.503, graph-edit -0.329. Concept set methods 0.508-0.539.
limits: Judge scores novelty relative to the agent's own earlier episodes only (comparative task), not absolute. Rubric levels are coarse. Single judge family at the top.
agent_relevance: A model judge can rate 'new approach vs earlier attempts' fairly well when it sees all prior attempts, but it is costly. Embedding distance is a cheaper proxy; keep novelty counted by code where possible (G8).

source: Bhushan, Zhang, Wang (2026) Can LLM Agents Discover? Evaluating Creativity on ML Engineering Tasks
finding: Bias checks on the GPT-5 novelty judge found no length, position or self-preference bias.
numbers: Partial correlation of judge error with plan length -0.032 (p=0.585), code length -0.074 (p=0.201); with episode position -0.041 (p=0.482) and +0.049 (p=0.402). Prompt ablation: full 0.732, no examples 0.684, no edge rules 0.699, no procedure 0.712. Self-preference test: GPT-5 minus DeepSeek gap was +0.129 on own outputs vs +0.300 on Qwen outputs (p=0.000038), so GPT-5 was harsher on itself.
limits: Only GPT-5 and DeepSeek V3.2 compared. The self-preference test uses a neutral judge that has its own bias. Contradicts the general self-preference literature, so do not generalize.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence that a strong judge can be made unbiased on a narrow rubric. G5 still applies: treat judge scores as a hint.

source: Bhushan, Zhang, Wang (2026) Can LLM Agents Discover? Evaluating Creativity on ML Engineering Tasks
finding: Across human and LLM agents, creativity falls and performance rises over iterations. Agents shift from exploration to exploitation faster than humans. Change in novelty and change in score are nearly uncorrelated.
numbers: Spearman of per-episode change in impact vs change in P-creativity: human -0.111 (p<0.05), AIDE GPT-5 -0.021, AIDE Qwen3-32B 0.056, AIRA Qwen3-32B -0.026. Reasoning-trace labels (AIDE Qwen3-32B): strategic exploration about 75% of behaviours early, 25% at the end; parametric refinement 15% to over 50%. 8 runs per task per model, max 10 episodes, 8-hour budget.
limits: Max 10 episodes per run. Labels for behaviour types come from a DeepSeek classifier, not humans. Kaggle tabular and vision tasks only.
agent_relevance: Supports: exploration is front-loaded and then dies. If S3 open mode is to produce distinct ideas, the program must force the spread early and keep it, since models will drift to refining the first working idea.

source: Bhushan, Zhang, Wang (2026) Can LLM Agents Discover? Evaluating Creativity on ML Engineering Tasks
finding: Search policy did not change creativity or impact much: greedy, MCTS and evolutionary variants converged within a few episodes.
numbers: AIRA-Dojo with Qwen3-32B on 3 tasks, 4 runs each for greedy and evolutionary, 8 for MCTS. All three drop below P-creativity 1 within the first few episodes. Greedy starts highest in P-creativity and also reaches the highest impact.
limits: 3 tasks only, small runs. Authors conclude the scaffolding (how solutions are mutated, how context passes) dominates the policy.
agent_relevance: The generator and context handling matter more than the selection rule. Which generator to use for S3: do not expect tree search alone to rescue diversity.

source: Bhushan, Zhang, Wang (2026) Can LLM Agents Discover? Evaluating Creativity on ML Engineering Tasks
finding: Agents explore regions humans did not, but this does not buy performance. GPT-5 is far more historically novel than gold-medal humans; Qwen3-32B is not.
numbers: H-creativity (0-4 scale) of post-competition medal human solutions: gold 0.744, silver 0.524, bronze 0.293. AIDE GPT-5 1.423 (p<1e-15 vs gold). AIDE Qwen3-32B 0.838 (p=0.33), AIRA Qwen3-32B 0.800 (p=0.99). Medal rate: 21.25% of GPT-5 runs, 10.85% of AIDE Qwen3-32B runs. Cross-task control episodes scored 2.39 (so in-task novelty is directed, not random).
limits: H-creativity uses retrieval of nearest human notebooks plus an LLM judge on 877-3,747 notebooks per task; the human corpus may miss unpublished methods. Novelty and usefulness correlate positively among humans (higher medal tier, higher novelty) but not for agents.
agent_relevance: Novelty alone is a weak selection signal. Pair any novelty selection with a code-run check of usefulness (G3, G8).

source: Sun et al. (2025) OMEGA: Can LLMs Reason Outside the Box in Math? Evaluating Exploratory, Compositional, and Transformative Generalization
finding: Benchmark with three axes inspired by Boden: exploratory (harder instances of a known skill), compositional (combine two learned skills), transformative (abandon the familiar tactic). Frontier reasoning models decline sharply as complexity rises. RL helps exploratory, barely helps compositional, and does not help transformative.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, GRPO on 1k problems per setting. Zebra Logic: base 30%, then +61 points in-distribution and +53 points out-of-distribution. Geometry: base under 15%, +31 pp ID but only +8 pp OOD. Arithmetic GCD: level 3 from 6% to 10%; level 5 stays 3% even when levels 1-4 are trained. Polygon rotation base 13%, about +70 pp on the isolated skill; composition does not follow. Transformative OOD accuracy stays near zero in most settings; in matrix rank, RL reversed a high base result.
limits: Only small open models were fine-tuned. Problems come from generators with verified answers, so 'transformative' means 'needs a different tactic than the one trained', a narrow reading of Boden. Axis labels are the authors' mapping, not a test of Boden's theory.
agent_relevance: The closest controlled evidence that exploring within a trained style is learnable while changing style is not. Transformation must come from the scaffold (operators that change the problem frame), not from hoping the model does it.

source: Sun et al. (2025) OMEGA
finding: More samples help only at moderate complexity. Failure at higher complexity is partly lazy search, not only arithmetic slips.
numbers: Pass@k for k=1 to 32 on letter-distribution problems rises toward 100% at low complexity, falls to zero at complexity level 6 even at 64 attempts. A DP solver needs only 36 states at that level. In matrix rank, share of CoT spent on real computation drops from about 65% at level 1 to under 40% at level 7 while conjecture share grows; per-step arithmetic accuracy stays high.
limits: One model (DeepSeek-R1) for the trace analysis; labels from o4-mini. 64-attempt cap.
agent_relevance: Voting or best-of-N over one model cannot reach what that model never explores (G4). A transformed problem (new representation, e.g. DP) must be supplied by an operator.

source: Wang et al. (2026) CreativeBench: Benchmarking and Enhancing Machine Creativity via Self-Evolving Challenges
finding: Code benchmark with a Combo (combinational) subset and an Explore (exploratory) subset. Creativity score is quality (Pass@1) times novelty (embedding plus n-gram distance). Scaling helps combination much more than exploration. Larger models are more correct but less divergent ('convergence-by-scaling').
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct vanilla: Combo Pass@1 9.21%, creativity 0.168; Explore Pass@1 4.11%, creativity 0.0146. Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite vanilla: Combo 36.41%, creativity 0.509; Explore 23.51%, creativity 0.1681. Best model (Gemini-3-Pro) under 60% Pass@1 on both subsets. Means over N=10 runs. Reasoning mode gives almost no gain on Combo but significant gain on Explore.
limits: Novelty is embedding distance from a reference solution, a weak proxy. Datasets built by LLM pipelines (reverse engineering, self-play), so benchmark creativity may be bounded by the building model. Code domain only.
agent_relevance: Strong hint for S3: a bigger or newer model is not a better generator of distinct ideas. Reasoning helps constrained exploration, so use thinking mode for exploratory search with explicit constraints.

source: Wang et al. (2026) CreativeBench
finding: Evolutionary search (AlphaEvolve-style, GEPA) raises creativity only a little on a 7B model; an inference-time steering vector (EvoRePE) adds a small, consistent gain on top, even without evolution.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B Combo: vanilla creativity 0.168, +EvoRePE 0.174; AlphaEvolve 0.175, +EvoRePE 0.193; GEPA 0.188. Explore: vanilla 0.0146, AlphaEvolve 0.0163 (+EvoRePE 0.0169), GEPA 0.0182. Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite Combo: vanilla 0.509, AlphaEvolve 0.605, evolutionary 0.567 (Pass@1 36.4% to 39.0% for AlphaEvolve). Stable steering window alpha 0.05-0.45; 0.5 breaks Pass@1.
limits: Needs white-box activations, so not usable on an API agent. Gains are small in absolute terms on Explore (0.0146 to 0.018).
agent_relevance: Evolutionary search over a population gives a modest, repeatable gain. Steering is out of reach for a scaffold-only agent.

source: Suzuki, Banaei-Kashani (2026) Universe of Thoughts: A Computational Framework for Creative Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Turns Boden's three types into three executable operators (combinational C-UoT, exploratory E-UoT, transformational T-UoT, where T edits the rules that define the space). Which one wins depends on how constrained the task is.
numbers: HypoArena, 100 tasks, Qwen3-14B: E-UoT average BTD 1535.4, pairwise win rate 32.7%; next best ToT 1515.8 and 25.5%; OnePrompt 1475.7 and 14.3%; CoT 18.8%; C-UoT 19.5%; T-UoT 17.3%. Ablations (full vs ablated, chance 50%): C-UoT 58.3%, T-UoT 54.2%, E-UoT 52.4%. Per-task: C-UoT top on 15/100 tasks, T-UoT on 11/100. Token cost per task: OnePrompt 3.7k, ToT 27.1k, E-UoT 36.7k, C-UoT 134.3k, T-UoT 193.3k. GLM-4-9B: OnePrompt ranked first, E-UoT best structured method.
limits: LLM judges (Gemma primary; two others agree, kappa 0.59-0.79; hard reversals 2.6-5.4%). Human-automated agreement only r=0.708 at method level on the authors' own three tasks. Backbone-dependent. T-UoT cost is 52 times plain prompting, and in the stage diagnosis only 13-16% of rewritten rules survive into the final answer.
agent_relevance: Direct test of 'which generator for S3'. In a constrained task use exploratory search; transformation pays off only on some tasks at high cost. Gate transformation on an impasse signal (G1) rather than running it by default.

source: Suzuki, Banaei-Kashani (2026) Universe of Thoughts
finding: On the authors' three low-constraint tasks (Bridge, Electricity, Society), the transformational mode is best on the two with specific objectives and the combinational mode best on the vague-objective one.
numbers: 10 generations per method per task with GPT-4o; stage diagnosis: C-UoT analogy selected 100%, mapped-mechanism specificity 0.97, but 'strong transfer' only 52% (when C beats ToT) vs 32% (when it loses); T-UoT gate passed 100%, rule transform applied 75% (wins) vs 83% (losses).
limits: Very small samples (10 generations per cell), authors' own tasks, LLM-judged. The pattern is a hypothesis, not a replication.
agent_relevance: The type of task (constrained vs not, specific objective vs vague) is the moderator to record. S3 should choose the generator from those two features.

source: Chakrabarty et al. (2024) Art or Artifice? LLMs and the False Promise of Creativity
finding: Expert writers judged 48 stories with 14 binary Torrance-style tests. LLM stories passed 3-10 times fewer tests than New Yorker stories. LLM judges did not agree with experts.
numbers: 10 experts, 48 stories. New Yorker stories pass 84.7% of tests (11.9 of 14). GPT-3.5 stories under 10%; GPT-4 and Claude v1.3 about 30%. No LLM-administered TTCW correlated positively with expert annotations (Cohen's kappa table).
limits: 2023 models, single prompt style, professional benchmark is the strongest possible comparison. Not replicated with 2026 models in this document.
agent_relevance: Baseline for 'LLM output is competent but not original' and a reason G8 forbids model self-selection of novelty.

source: Luo, King, Puett, Smith (2026) Inducing Sustained Creativity and Diversity in LLMs
finding: A cheap decoding trick (inserting random token prefixes so the model continues from an unusual start) produces many more distinct ideas than ordinary decoding, and keeps going for 1,000 runs. Better models do worse under ordinary decoding.
numbers: 50 topics, 4 LLMs. Cluster test: random-prefix method (RD) 244 clusters from 250 ideas vs 35 for ordinary decoding (OD) on one image topic. Across 5 datasets x 3 models, mean LLM-rated diversity 0.68 (RD) vs 0.33 (OD), relevance 0.98 vs 0.99. GPT-5.1: 0.27 to 0.70 (+161.2%); Gemini-3: 0.27 to 0.65 (+140.1%). RD3 covers about 100% of OD3 clusters, OD3 covers only 30-40% of RD3 clusters. Embedding-based diversity: RD 95.0%, VS (verbalized sampling) 85.0%, human 82.0%, OD3 15.0%. Relevance check: 80% majority-vote agreement on 500 sampled responses.
limits: Diversity measured by clustering and LLM raters; clustering threshold shapes results. Chat APIs needed a simulated completion prompt, with some loss. Not a test of Boden's types, but of how to reach other parts of the space.
agent_relevance: A strong, cheap generator trick for S3 that uses no judge: diversify the start of the generation, then count clusters in code.

source: Schapiro, Sosa, Park, Varshney (2026) CreativityNeuro: Steering LM Weights to Improve Divergent Thinking and Reduce Mode Collapse
finding: Weight steering raises human-rated originality and surprise, with a cost in utility, and beats activation steering on transfer to unseen tasks.
numbers: DAT: up to +14 human percentile points. Human evaluation N=720 reviewers. AUT originality average d=+0.36 over six models (four significant); surprise d=+0.43 (five significant); utility fell. Task Task originality d=+0.40 (Phi-14B +0.61, Qwen-14B +0.56), creativity d=+0.24. DAT: activation steering 93.9 vs weight steering 94.1 average percentile; activation steering did not transfer to AUT or Task Task.
limits: Needs weights access. Small to medium effects. Novelty-utility tradeoff is explicit.
agent_relevance: Confirms that novelty raised by model-side means costs utility; a scaffold must re-check usefulness in code.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models
finding: Large study (26K real open-ended queries, 70+ models, 31,250 human annotations) argues that models repeat themselves and each other on open-ended prompts.
numbers: In 79% of cases the average same-model response similarity exceeds 0.8 (embedding cosine); same-prompt similarity typically exceeds 0.8. 25 human annotations per example. LMs, reward models and LM judges are less well calibrated on items where annotators disagree.
limits: Contested: see the re-evaluation in b16. No human baseline for homogeneity; the 0.8 threshold has no null. Embedding similarity may measure sharing a prompt.
agent_relevance: Taken at face value it says exploratory search by repeated sampling stays in one basin (G4). Weigh with b16 before building a mechanism on it.

source: Schaeffer, Miranda, Kazdan, Chudnovsky, Koyejo (2026) How Strong Is the Evidence for the Artificial Hivemind?
finding: A critical re-evaluation (not a full replication) says the homogeneity evidence does not hold up as stated: the flagship example is not two clusters, the null is too weak, and prompting does raise diversity.
numbers: Under a stricter null (same-prompt responses expressing different ideas), 20%-32% of pairs already exceed the 0.8 threshold; the original same-prompt pairs exceed it only about 2-3 times as often. Flagship 'time metaphor' prompt shows one dominant vehicle plus a heavy tail of minority vehicles; authors say 'time' is one of their least diverse topics. No human baseline in the original; model-indistinguishability statistic has no null. Authors do not claim hivemind is false.
limits: Preprint, short time since original, only a subset of the original claims re-examined. Prompting raises measured diversity, which the authors say is not the same as human-valued creativity.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on a claim that models cannot vary; use prompt-level variation plus code-side clustering. Always compare diversity to a null.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Blind expert review found LLM ideas more novel but a little less feasible than human expert ideas. The generator runs out of distinct ideas quickly, and LLM self-evaluation fails.
numbers: 49 human and 49 AI ideas (79 reviewers). Novelty: human 4.84 (SD 1.79, n=119 reviews) vs AI 5.64 (SD 1.76, n=109), p<0.01; AI + human rerank 5.81. Excitement 4.55 vs 5.19 (p=0.04); rerank 5.46. Of 4000 generated seed ideas, only about 200 were non-duplicates (cosine similarity threshold 0.8, about 5%). Reviewer agreement only 56.1% (vs 66.0% NeurIPS 2021 consistency, 71.9% ICLR 2024 LM submissions).
limits: Novelty judged by reviewers, not by running the idea. Agreement near chance for ideas; one prompting setup; 7 NLP topics. The execution follow-up is cited by b01 as showing novelty and effectiveness decouple.
agent_relevance: Two lessons: raw LLM ideation hits a ceiling of duplicates (dedupe in code), and novelty ratings from humans are noisy (agreement 56.1%).

source: Franceschelli, Musolesi (2024) On the Creativity of Large Language Models
finding: Argues that LLMs might at most show combinational or exploratory creativity, and that transformational creativity is not reachable with present training. Adds 'B-novelty' (novel to the beholder) to explain why outputs still feel creative.
numbers: No empirical test. Position: autoregressive training on a given distribution plus RLHF or DPO reduces diversity.
limits: Argument by theory. Later evidence (b06 transformative near zero, b10 T-UoT helps on some tasks only) is mixed; nobody has shown transformation by an LLM against a fixed rule set.
agent_relevance: The claim a scaffold should test: does an operator that edits the rules (O4/O6 style) yield results the model's sampler never gives?

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Computational creativity (Boden and Wiggins sections)
finding: Summary of Boden's three types and that Boden's ideas were formalised mostly by Geraint Wiggins (2006). Jordanous and Keller gathered 694 creativity words from 60 years of empirical studies into 14 components (SPECS).
numbers: Only first 100,000 of 124,305 characters were read. The page reports no experimental effect sizes.
quote: creativity that arises from an exploration within an established conceptual space
limits: Tertiary source; no figures. Ritchie's criteria were not covered in the part read.
agent_relevance: Use only as pointer; nothing here is evidence of effect.

source: Boden (1990/1998/2004) The Creative Mind: Myths and Mechanisms; Creativity and artificial intelligence (Artif. Intell. 103)
finding: Founding theory: combinational, exploratory and transformational creativity; P-creative vs H-creative. Transformation changes the rules of the conceptual space, so previously impossible ideas become possible.
numbers: none opened; no experiment in the founding text
limits: Cited and quoted in sources I opened (b01, b06, b08, b18), but I did not open the original. It is a conceptual theory, not tested by controlled human experiments in anything I read. The boundary between exploring and transforming is itself contested.
agent_relevance: Source of the three-way split used for S3 generator choice.

source: Wiggins (2006) A preliminary framework for description, analysis and comparison of creative systems
finding: Formalises Boden's types as search over a universal set with rules for the space, traversal and evaluation; exploratory means searching within the rules, transformational means searching the rules. Named in b19 as the main formalisation.
numbers: none opened
limits: Not opened. Details here are from memory and are unconfirmed. Formal model, with no experiment attached.
agent_relevance: Gives a vocabulary: space (rules R), traversal (T), evaluation (E). Transformation = change of R or T.

source: Ritchie (2007) Some empirical criteria for attributing creativity to a computer program
finding: Proposed measurable criteria (typicality of output, value, and ratios between them) to decide if a program is creative, which are used in later system comparisons.
numbers: none opened
limits: Not opened. Cited from memory, unconfirmed. No numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: A test that judges the output set, not the method; matches our idea of a code-side check.

source: Lehman, Stanley (2011) Abandoning objectives: evolution through the search for novelty alone
finding: Novelty search (reward behavioural difference, not the objective) can solve deceptive tasks where objective-driven search stalls. Cited in b08 as part of the evolutionary-systems measurement problem.
numbers: none opened
limits: Not opened. From memory, unconfirmed. Complementary evidence is the quality-diversity line (MAP-Elites), also not opened.
agent_relevance: Selection by distance to archive is a code-side, judge-free exploratory method for S3.

source: Bhushan et al. (2026) citing Beaty et al. (2026) AGC-Bench
finding: Second-hand: the COLM paper says AGC-Bench reviewed over 3,000 papers and tested 83 LLMs, finding that creativity forms a coherent factor separable from general reasoning.
numbers: Numbers as cited: more than 3,000 papers, 83 LLMs.
limits: I read only the citing sentence, not Beaty et al. Do not rely on it until the original is opened.
agent_relevance: If true, a bigger reasoner is not a more creative one, matching b08 convergence-by-scaling.

source: Bhushan et al. (2026) citing Lu et al. (2026) and Si et al. (2025) execution audit
finding: Second-hand: automated novelty metrics favour stylistic over conceptual novelty and shift under minor prompt variation; idea novelty and execution effectiveness decouple once ideas are run.
numbers: No numbers given in the citing text.
limits: Only the citing paper's summary was read.
agent_relevance: Reason to keep a run-based check on ideas and to fix prompt wording when measuring novelty.

source: Chakrabarty et al. (2024) Art or Artifice
finding: Experts identified specific 'AI tics' that mark low originality: topic sentence plus summary sentence, ornamental figurative language, moralizing tone. Experts may find it easier to spot low-quality machine text than low-quality human text.
numbers: Qualitative; 10 experts; pass-rate numbers in b12.
limits: Interpretive. No effect size for the tic claims.
agent_relevance: Gives surface cues that a code check could count (summary closers, moral lines) as cheap non-judge penalties.

source: Luo et al. (2026) Inducing Sustained Creativity
finding: Boundary condition: diversity gain is capped by the size of the true answer space. Topics with finite answer sets (fashion accessories) flatten while open ones (advertising campaign) stay near-linear to run 1,000.
numbers: 1,000 runs over 50 topics; RD3 growth stays near linear on open topics. Mean relevance 0.98 vs 0.99.
limits: Descriptive; the authors do not give a numerical cut-off. Cluster counts depend on a distance threshold.
agent_relevance: Stop condition for S3: when cluster growth flattens, quit generating and move on.
